I independently re-queried Google Books search-within-volume (most queries were rate-could not be reached by automated download, but two got through and are now saved beside the original with updated): (1) query "negative prefix" -> p. 28 '.. or as [ painũ ] without any change of meaning. 2.2.4 Tone and stress The…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the first syllable of the word; the negative prefix ma- does not take the stress (so in negated verbs stress presumably falls on the following, stem-initial syllable -- the continuation of the sentence was not visible).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing visible in the accessible snippet.
new_statements.exceptions: Words whose first syllable is the negative prefix <ma-> (NEG) are exempt from initial stress (sentence truncated after '(NEG').
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for 'words' in general (word-level rule) in the phonology chapter of a grammar based on the author's fieldwork; the same section heading covers tone, but the tone part of sec. 2.2.4 was not visible. Older SIL work (Bieri & Schulze 1970/1971, Sabra dialect) treats the word as a pitch unit whose contour is set by the first syllable, without an explicit stress rule; Rapacha 2005 (Katunje dialect) discusses only tone (arguing it is lost there) and never mentions stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Borchers 2008 describes Sunwar (Kiranti-Kõits, sunw1242) from her own fieldwork in the Sunwar home area of eastern Nepal (Likhu/Khimti valleys; exact villages not visible in the open front matter). The older SIL material (Bieri & Schulze 1969-71, in Hale & Pike 1970) is the Sabra village dialect, Likhu valley, Ramechhap; Genetti 1988 / DeLancey 1992 use a Khiji (Okhaldhunga) speaker; Rapacha 2005 describes the Katunje dialect (Okhaldhunga) and claims it has lost contrastive tone; Baskaran 2009 describes diaspora Sunwar in Sikkim. All are the same Glottolog language sunw1242; none is Surel/Jirel.

tone_statements.quote: The first syllable of a word is the most important one and carries a high or low tone (tones are not marked in texts, they are known by meaning). A closed syllable carries a contour tone, an open syllable a register tone. [...] Nasalisation and laryngealisation or a fricative are analysed as syllable closure. The first closed syllable of a word carries a contour tone. The syllable closure can be /m/, /l/, or /r/, a lenis glottal stop, nasalisation, laryngealisation or fricative. [p. 7:] The high register or contour tone is marked in the Dictionary with apostrophe. The low tone is unmarked.

tone_statements.quote: Sunuwar is a pronominalised language without inclusive and exclusive in pronoun system and it is reported to be tonal (van Driem 2001: 725). Tonality is not the feature of Rai-Kirati languages and Sunuwar it is unlikely to be a tonal language. Simialrly, Rapacha (2005) has identified it as a word stressed language. These claims are to be verified because stress is not the feature of Rai-Kirati languages, too.

tone_statements.citation: Michailovsky, Boyd. 1988. Phonological typology of Nepal languages. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 11(2): 25-50. doi:10.15144/LTBA-11.2.25
tone_statements.quote: In the pronominalized languages of East Nepal, tone is reported from a clearly defined area including Sunwar, Khaling, probably Sotang and Kulung, and (problematically) Thulung. All of these languages have distinctive voicing and aspiration of initial stops on all tones; some have murmur as well. In Sunwar and Khaling, and tentatively in Sotang and Kulung, two-tone systems are reported. Phonetically, the exponents of these systems are high and low pitch; their domain is the word. In Sunwar, the opposition is neutralized on monosyliables.

tone_statements.n_tones: 2 (high vs low pitch), as reported; opposition neutralized on monosyllables

sources.note: Sabra dialect (Ramechhap). sources.citation: Genetti, Carol. 1992. Segmental alternations in the Sunwari verb stem: a case for the feature [front]. Linguistics 30(2): 319-358. Berlin/New York: Walter de Gruyter. doi:10.1515/ling.1992.30.2.319
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: Sunwari is a tone language. In the Sunwari verb there is a two-way distinction between high and low tone. These tones will be marked by the indices H and L following the cited form: [...] Tone contour (a distinction between level and falling) is predictable in Sunwari verbs: it falls in bimoraic syllables and is level in monomoraic syllables. [...] Both pitch (high/low) and contour (level/falling) are distinctive in Sunwari nouns and are freely independent of syllable type, so both will be marked in all instances: kodz LL 'belly' / kyodz HL 'barley'; mor LL 'monkey' / mur HL 'man'; baas LL 'floor' / blaas LF 'broom'; naa LF 'sun' / naa LL 'previously'; bus HF 'owl' / bus HL 'snake'.

sources.quote: In the pronominalized languages of East Nepal, tone is reported from a clearly defined area including Sunwar, Khaling, probably Sotang and Kulung, and (problematically) Thulung. All of these languages have distinctive voicing and aspiration of initial stops on all tones; some have murmur as well. In Sunwar and Khaling, and tentatively in Sotang and Kulung, two-tone systems are reported. Phonetically, the exponents of these systems are high and low pitch; their domain is the word. In Sunwar, the opposition is neutralized on monosyliables.

sources.quote: The analysis of tone is incomplete. There is a clear contrast between contour tone and register tone. The contour tone occurs as high falling and low falling. The register tone contrasts as high and low. Tone seems to be relevant on a higher level than the syllable level and will be described in a later paper. Tone does not influence or condition the contrasts of the phonemes described elsewhere in this report.
